newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Moslem group says Taleban deny threatening Buddhas.
newsitem.headline: Moslem group says Taleban deny threatening Buddhas.

text.p: Afghanistan's fundamentalist Taleban movement has denied any plans to destroy two giant statues of Buddha, a spokesman for the World Muslim Congress said on Friday.

"I contacted the Taleban leadership and it has categorically refuted the news terming it false, fabricated and part of a propaganda against the Taleban Government," said Raja Zafarul Haq, the Pakistani secretary general of the Saudi-funded group.

Haq was quoted by the official APP news agency as saying he had contacted Taleban leadership on the matter on the request of Moslem communities in Buddhist-populated Sri Lanka and some Far Eastern countries.

He said Moslems in those countries were alarmed after news reports quoted a Taleban commander as saying the purist Islamic militia would destroy the statues in the central province of Bamiyan after capturing the area from an opposition faction.
Haq said the Moslem communities had asked him to intervene because they feared the reported threat to destroy the 1,500-year-old statues would create a backlash from Buddhist communities.
Haq said the Taleban leadership had made it clear to him that it had no intention to pull down the statues and that Islam does not permit desecration of religious sites of other faiths.

The two huge 4th century Buddhas of Bamiyan, one 38 metres (125 feet) high and the other 55 metres (180 feet) high -- the tallest standing Buddha in the world -- were carved out of a sandstone cliff in central Afghanistan when Europe was deep in the dark ages.
Taleban commander Ahmadzai, whose forces are trying to take the Bamiyan area, told journalists last week: "We will destroy them because Islam has forbidden statues."
Taleban authorities in Kabul said the commander had no authority to make such a threat, which sparked fresh concern for the country's cultural heritage.
The threat prompted United Nations secretary-general Kofi Annan to appeal on Thursday to political and military commanders in Afghanistan to ensure that no harm comes to the statues.
India and Sri Lanka have also expressed concern.
Afghanistan has been a cross-roads of cultures and religions for thousands of years and each has left its mark.

But even Ghenghis Khan, possibly the greatest vandal of all time, whose troops rampaged through Asia seven hundred years ago levelling some of the greatest civilisations of the period, was unable to do as much damage to Afghanistan's history and heritage as the last 20 years of war in the country.

Greek cities founded by Alexander the Great that had lain undisturbed for centuries, apart from the delicate attentions of archaeologists' trowels, are now being flattened to improve access for treasure hunters.
